results.summary: This project implements an 8-bit Kogge-Stone adder in Verilog. It takes two 8-bit inputs and produces their sum, but lacks a carry-out so sums above 255 are not representable. The design is intended as a class exercise and includes a testbench that iterates through all input combinations, skipping cases where overflow would occur. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.

This design is a nibble-serial implementation of the LED block cipher, which encrypts a 64-bit plaintext block using a 128-bit key. It serializes both data input and output to fit within the limited I/O pins, controlled by a simple handshake protocol. The cipher requires external hardware, such as a Raspberry Pi, to provide the serial data and control signals. The design is notable for its compact implementation, reusing datapath logic across nibbles, at the cost of increased latency.

This project drives a 32x8 LED matrix using a MAX7219/7221 controller via SPI. It displays an animation that alternates between a beaver logo and the letters 'BWSI', with bitmaps stored in an internal ROM. The design is intended to be tested on an FPGA connected to a breadboard, requiring external hardware including the LED matrix, the MAX7219/7221 chip, and a 5V power source. The SPI interface handles both configuration and bitmap data transmission.

This design implements a fuzzy search engine based on the bit-vector Levenshtein distance algorithm. It finds the closest matching word in a dictionary stored in external QSPI PSRAM, communicating with the host via SPI. The design requires a specific QSPI PSRAM PMOD that supports quad-mode operations and runs at half the clock speed of the chip. It is notable for being a hardware implementation of a string matching algorithm, with a provided client tool for testing.

This project implements an 8-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) that generates a pseudo-random sequence. It accepts an 8-bit seed value and a write-enable signal to load the seed, and outputs the current LFSR state on eight output pins. The design is simple and requires no external hardware beyond reading the output pins. It can be used as a basic pseudo-random number generator.

This project simulates a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit input current and updates an internal state variable, producing a spike output when the state exceeds a threshold. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed usage or testing instructions. No external hardware is required.

This project implements a spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) circuit in Verilog. It detects pre- and post-synaptic spikes, measures the time difference between them, and adjusts a synaptic weight using an exponential trace model. The design is still under development and testing is incomplete. No external hardware is required.

This project is a tutorial implementation of a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit input current and updates an internal state variable, producing a spike output when the state exceeds a threshold. The documentation is very sparse, with only a brief description and no detailed testing instructions. No external hardware is required.

This project implements a single-layer perceptron in Verilog. It takes 8 bits of input and 8 bits of weights, and classifies the input into one of two classes based on a weighted sum and threshold. The design is tested using a Python script that initializes inputs and expected outputs, and then runs a makefile-based test. No external hardware is required.

This project implements a small spiking neural network based on the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model. It consists of three input neurons that receive 5-bit input currents, and one output neuron that integrates weighted spikes from the input neurons. The design can be tested in simulation or on an FPGA, with LEDs and switches for input and output. It is suitable for basic pattern recognition or response simulations.
